facts.fact: Warren Hastings became the first Governor-General of Bengal under the Regulating Act of 1773.
Lord Wellesley introduced the Subsidiary Alliance system.
Lord Canning was the first Viceroy of India.
Lord William Bentinck abolished Sati (1829) and became the first Governor-General of India.
The Government of India Act 1858 abolished the East India Company and transferred power to the Crown.
The first Census (1872) and financial decentralisation came under Lord Mayo.
Lytton passed the Vernacular Press Act and the Arms Act.
The INC was founded in 1885 under Lord Dufferin.
Curzon partitioned Bengal (1905) and passed the Indian Universities Act.
The Morley-Minto Reforms (1909) introduced separate electorates under Minto II.
Hardinge II annulled the Bengal partition and shifted the capital to Delhi.
The Dandi March and the first Round Table Conference came under Irwin.
Mountbatten proposed the June 3rd Plan and was the last Viceroy and first GG of free India.
The Subsidiary Alliance did not aim to secure a fixed income for the Company.
The Butler Committee (1927) examined relations between the Crown and the Indian States.
The Rowlatt Act and Jallianwala Bagh (1919) came during Chelmsford's viceroyalty.
Dalhousie introduced the Doctrine of Lapse and the first railway.
Cornwallis introduced the Permanent Settlement and is called the Father of Civil Services.
Ripon introduced the Ilbert Bill.
Ryotwari is associated with Read and Munro; Mahalwari with Holt Mackenzie.
Warren Hastings was Governor of Bengal from 1772 and Governor-General of Bengal 1773–1785.
The Supreme Court at Fort William (Calcutta) was set up in 1774 with Elijah Impey as Chief Justice.
Hastings lent troops to Awadh for the Rohilla War (1774).
Raja Nand Kumar, who accused Hastings of bribery, was hanged for forgery in 1775.
Hastings founded the Calcutta Madrasa in 1781.
The Asiatic Society of Bengal was founded in 1784 by William Jones under Hastings’s patronage.
Charles Wilkins made the first English translation of the Bhagavad Gita (1785) under Hastings.
Hastings was impeached in Britain (led by Edmund Burke) over Chait Singh and the Begums of Awadh; acquitted in 1795.
Hastings moved the treasury from Murshidabad to Calcutta and set up district Diwani and Faujdari Adalats (1772).
Sir John Macpherson was acting Governor-General in 1785–86.
Lord Cornwallis was Governor-General 1786–1793.
The Cornwallis Code (1793) separated revenue from judicial administration.
Cornwallis organised districts into thanas under a daroga.
Sir John Shore (1793–98) followed non-intervention; the Battle of Kharda (1795), where the Marathas beat the Nizam, came in his time.
The Charter Act of 1793 was passed under Sir John Shore.
Wellesley called himself the Bengal Tiger; the Nizam (1798) was the first to sign his subsidiary alliance.
Wellesley imposed press censorship by the Censorship of Press Act (1799).
The Madras Presidency was organised under Wellesley (1801).
The Vellore Mutiny (10 July 1806) broke out under Sir George Barlow.
Lord Minto I (1807–13) concluded the Treaty of Amritsar (1809) with Ranjit Singh.
Lord Hastings (Marquess of Hastings, Lord Moira) was Governor-General 1813–1823.
Lord Hastings ended non-intervention and adopted a policy of intervention and war (paramountcy).
The Anglo-Nepal War (1814–16) ended with the Treaty of Sagauli (1816).
Lord Hastings crushed the Pindaris and the Marathas, abolishing the Peshwaship (1818).
Thomas Munro introduced ryotwari in Madras (1820) under Lord Hastings.
John Adam, acting Governor-General (1823), imposed the Licensing Regulation of 1823 on the press.
The First Anglo-Burmese War (1824–26) under Amherst ended with the Treaty of Yandabo (1826).
Under the Treaty of Yandabo Assam passed to the British.
Sepoys refusing to go to Burma mutinied at Barrackpore in 1824 under Amherst.
Amherst captured Bharatpur in 1826.
The Sanskrit College at Calcutta was founded in 1824 under Amherst.
Lord William Bentinck was Governor-General 1828–1835 (of India from 1833).
Sati was banned by Bengal Regulation XVII of 4 December 1829.
Bentinck suppressed the thugs (1830s) through Colonel William Sleeman.
Bentinck took over Mysore’s administration (1831) and annexed Coorg (1834).
Macaulay's Minute (2 Feb 1835) led to Bentinck's English Education Act (1835).
The Calcutta Medical College was founded in 1835 under Bentinck.
Charles Metcalfe (1835–36) repealed the 1823 Licensing Regulation and is called the Liberator of the Indian Press.
The Calcutta Public Library was opened in 1836 under Metcalfe.
Lord Auckland (1836–42) began the First Anglo-Afghan War (1838–42), a disaster for British prestige.
The Tripartite Treaty (1838) of the British, Shah Shuja and Ranjit Singh aimed to oust Dost Muhammad (the PDF lists it under Ellenborough).
Lord Ellenborough (1842–44) annexed Sindh (1843) after Charles Napier’s victory.
Slavery was abolished in India by Act V of 1843 under Ellenborough.
Lord Hardinge I (1844–48) fought the First Anglo-Sikh War (1845–46).
Lord Dalhousie (James Andrew Broun-Ramsay) was Governor-General 1848–1856.
Under the Doctrine of Lapse Dalhousie annexed Satara (1848), Jaitpur and Sambalpur (1849), Udaipur (1852), Jhansi (1853) and Nagpur (1854).
Dalhousie annexed Awadh (1856) on grounds of misgovernment, not lapse.
The Second Anglo-Burmese War (1852) gave Dalhousie Lower Burma (Pegu).
Dalhousie took Berar from the Nizam (1853) to pay for the subsidiary force.
The first railway ran from Bombay to Thane on 16 April 1853 (34 km).
Dalhousie laid about 4,000 miles of telegraph line linking Calcutta, Bombay, Madras and Peshawar.
The Post Office Act (1854) introduced uniform postage and postage stamps.
Dalhousie created a Public Works Department and opened the Ganges Canal (1854).
Dalhousie annexed Punjab (1849) after the Second Anglo-Sikh War.
Lord Canning was Governor-General 1856–58 and Viceroy 1858–62.
The Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act (26 July 1856) was enacted under Canning.
The General Service Enlistment Act (1856) — sepoys liable to serve overseas — came under Canning.
The Indian Penal Code (1860), drafted by Macaulay’s Law Commission, was enacted under Canning.
Income tax was first introduced in 1860 by James Wilson under Canning.
The 'White Mutiny' of the Company's European troops (1859) came under Canning.
The Indian High Courts Act (1861) was passed under Canning; the High Courts opened in 1862 under Elgin.
Lord Elgin I (1862–63) dealt with the Wahabi movement and died at Dharamsala.
High Courts at Calcutta, Bombay and Madras began in 1865 under Sir John Lawrence (1864–69).
The Anglo-Bhutanese (Duar) War of 1865 came under John Lawrence.
John Lawrence followed a policy of 'masterly inactivity' towards Afghanistan.
The Indian Forest Department was set up in 1864 under John Lawrence.
Lord Mayo (1869–72) began financial decentralisation between centre and provinces (1870).
Mayo College at Ajmer for princes is named after Lord Mayo.
Lord Mayo was killed by Sher Ali Afridi at Port Blair in 1872 — the only Viceroy assassinated in office.
Mayo created a Department of Agriculture and Commerce.
Lord Northbrook (1872–76) faced the Kuka (Namdhari) movement in Punjab.
The Prince of Wales (Edward VII) visited India in 1875–76 under Northbrook.
Malhar Rao Gaekwad of Baroda was tried and deposed (1875) under Northbrook.
Lytton held the Delhi Durbar on 1 January 1877 proclaiming Victoria Kaisar-i-Hind under the Royal Titles Act (1876).
The Vernacular Press Act (1878), the 'gagging act', was passed under Lytton.
The Great Famine (1876–78) led Lytton to appoint the Richard Strachey Famine Commission (1878).
The Second Anglo-Afghan War (1878–80) began under Lytton.
Lytton cut the ICS maximum age to 19 and created the Statutory Civil Service (1879).
Ripon's Resolution of 1882 on local self-government earned him the title Father of Local Self-Government.
The first Factory Act (1881) — child labour limits — came under Ripon.
The first synchronous all-India census was taken in 1881 under Ripon.
The Hunter Commission on education (1882) was appointed by Ripon.
Ripon repealed the Vernacular Press Act in 1882.
The Third Anglo-Burmese War (1885) and the annexation of Upper Burma (1886) came under Dufferin.
The Bengal Tenancy Act (1885) was passed under Dufferin.
The Indian Councils Act 1892 (indirect election) came under Lansdowne (1888–94).
The Durand Line (1893) between British India and Afghanistan was drawn under Lansdowne.
The Age of Consent Act (1891) was passed under Lansdowne.
The Chapekar brothers shot plague commissioner W.C. Rand at Poona (1897) under Elgin II.
The Lyall Famine Commission (1898) was set up under Elgin II.
Curzon appointed the Raleigh Commission (1902) on universities, leading to the Indian Universities Act (1904).
The Ancient Monuments Preservation Act (1904) revived the ASI under Curzon.
Curzon created the North-West Frontier Province (1901).
Curzon sent Younghusband's expedition to Tibet (1903–04).
The Police Commission under Andrew Fraser (1902) came under Curzon.
Curzon resigned (1905) after the Curzon–Kitchener controversy over army control.
The Partition of Bengal took effect on 16 October 1905.
The Calcutta Corporation Act (1899) cut elected members under Curzon.
The Agricultural Research Institute at Pusa was founded (1905) under Curzon.
The Muslim League was founded at Dacca on 30 December 1906 under Minto II.
The Surat Split of the Congress (1907) came under Minto II.
The Newspapers (Incitement to Offences) Act 1908 was passed under Minto II.
At the Delhi Durbar of 12 December 1911 George V announced the annulment of the partition and the capital shift to Delhi.
A bomb was thrown at Hardinge in Delhi (Chandni Chowk) on 23 December 1912 — the Delhi Conspiracy case.
The Ghadar Party (1913) and the Komagata Maru episode (1914) came under Hardinge II.
Gandhi returned to India (January 1915) and the Hindu Mahasabha was formed (1915) in Hardinge II's time.
The Lucknow Pact and the Home Rule Leagues (1916) came under Chelmsford.
Champaran (1917), Kheda and Ahmedabad (1918) satyagrahas occurred under Chelmsford.
The Saddler (Calcutta University) Commission (1917) was appointed under Chelmsford.
The Khilafat and Non-Cooperation movements (1920) began under Chelmsford.
The Moplah rebellion (1921) and the Prince of Wales visit (Nov 1921) came under Lord Reading.
Chauri Chaura (5 Feb 1922) and the Swaraj Party (1923) came under Reading.
Reading repealed the Rowlatt Act and the Press Act (1922).
The Kakori train robbery (1925) came under Reading.
The RSS (1925, Nagpur) and the Communist Party of India (1925, Kanpur) were founded under Reading.
The Simon Commission (1927) and the Butler Committee (1927) were appointed under Irwin.
Irwin's Deepavali Declaration (31 Oct 1929) promised dominion status as the goal.
The Sharda Act (Child Marriage Restraint Act, 1929) was passed under Irwin.
The Gandhi–Irwin Pact was signed on 5 March 1931.
The Communal Award (Aug 1932) and Poona Pact (Sept 1932) came under Willingdon.
The Government of India Act 1935 and the RBI (1935) came under Willingdon.
The Congress Socialist Party (1934) was formed under Willingdon.
Linlithgow (1936–43) had the longest viceroyalty.
Provincial elections under the 1935 Act were held in 1937.
The August Offer (1940) and the Lahore (Pakistan) Resolution (1940) came under Linlithgow.
The Quit India Movement began on 8 August 1942.
The Wavell Plan and the Shimla Conference were in June 1945.
The INA trials (1945) and the RIN Mutiny (Feb 1946) came under Wavell.
The Cabinet Mission came in March 1946 under Wavell.
Jinnah's Direct Action Day was 16 August 1946.
The Interim Government under Nehru took office on 2 September 1946.
The Indian Independence Act (18 July 1947) and the Radcliffe Award came under Mountbatten.
Mountbatten was Viceroy from March 1947 and Governor-General until June 1948.
C. Rajagopalachari (1948–50) was the first and last Indian Governor-General of India.
The Regulating Act 1773 gave the Governor-General of Bengal a council of four and set up a Supreme Court.
The Act of Settlement (1781) defined the jurisdiction of the Calcutta Supreme Court against the Council.
Pitt's India Act (1784) created the Board of Control — the system of dual control.
The Act of 1786 let Cornwallis overrule his council and be both GG and Commander-in-Chief.
The Charter Act 1793 renewed the Company’s monopoly for 20 years.
The Charter Act 1813 set aside Rs 1 lakh a year for education and opened India to missionaries.
The Charter Act 1833 added a law member (Macaulay) and set up the first Law Commission.
The Charter Act 1853 introduced open competition for the civil service and separated legislative from executive work.
The GoI Act 1858 created the Secretary of State for India with a 15-member Council of India.
The Permanent Settlement was proclaimed on 22 March 1793.
Under the Permanent Settlement the state took 10/11 of the rent; the zamindar kept 1/11.
The Sunset Law auctioned a zamindari if revenue was not paid by sunset of the due date.
John Shore advised Cornwallis on the Permanent Settlement.
Alexander Read first tried ryotwari in Baramahal (1792).
Ryotwari was extended to Bombay by Elphinstone and Wingate.
Ryotwari covered Madras, Bombay, Assam, Coorg and Berar.
Holt Mackenzie introduced Mahalwari by Regulation VII of 1822 in the North-Western Provinces.
Regulation IX of 1833 (Bird and Thomason) revised Mahalwari; R.M. Bird is called the father of land settlement in north India.
In Mahalwari the village (mahal) as a whole, through its headman, was the revenue unit, with periodic revision.
Jonathan Duncan founded the Sanskrit College at Benares in 1791.
Fort William College (1800) trained young British civil servants in Indian languages.
Hindu College, Calcutta (1817), was founded with David Hare’s support.
Wood's Dispatch (1854) proposed universities on the London model and grants-in-aid.
The Hunter Commission (1882) focused on primary and secondary education.
The Hartog Committee (1929) reported on education under Irwin.
The Butler Committee (1927) held that paramountcy must remain supreme.
The MacDonnell Famine Commission (1901) came under Curzon.
The Lee Commission (1923–24) dealt with Indianisation of the superior civil services.
The First Anglo-Afghan War (1839–42) ended with the massacre of the retreating British army (1842) and Dost Muhammad’s return.
The Treaty of Gandamak (1879) ended the first phase of the Second Afghan War under Lytton.
The Third Anglo-Afghan War (1919) under Chelmsford ended with the Treaty of Rawalpindi.
By the Treaty of Sagauli Nepal ceded Kumaon, Garhwal and Sikkim claims and accepted a British Resident at Kathmandu.
Upper Burma was annexed on 1 January 1886 after the Third Burmese War against King Thibaw.
